meaning: After a series of bad events, things end up in a terrible, ridiculous state.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form + 始末だ; この・あの + 始末だ

senses.label: End up (so badly)
senses.meaning: After listing a chain of bad events, states the final bad outcome. Like “and in the end, ... even ...” or “it's come to the point where ...”. It shows the speaker's frustration, resignation, or blame. Only for negative outcomes.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form / ている-form + 始末だ (often after 「〜し、〜し、挙げ句の果てに」, 「とうとう」, 「ついには」)
examples: My son never studies and just plays around, and now he's finally saying he'll quit school.
He kept coming in late, and in the end he even skipped work without notice.
Prices keep going up, and now I can't even afford enough vegetables.

senses.label: This is what it's come to
senses.meaning: 「この始末だ」 and 「あの始末だ」 point to the mess in front of you. Like “and look how it turned out”. Often used to scold others or mock oneself.
senses.connection: この／その／あの + 始末だ
examples: I warned you so many times, and look at this mess.
He said “leave it to me”, and look how that turned out.

notes: Only for bad outcomes. ✕「努力して、合格する始末だ」. For good outcomes use 「〜結果」 or 「〜ことになった」.
「始末する」 (to deal with), 「後始末」, 「始末書」, and 「始末が悪い」 (hard to handle) are noun or verb uses, not this pattern.
It sounds strongly disapproving. It's common in writing and complaints; don't use it to a superior's face.

daily.title: Complaining about a child
daily.description: A mother tells a friend her child is getting out of hand.
daily.example: Lately he just talks back, and yesterday he even said he'd run away from home.

daily.title: Laughing at a failed diet
daily.description: Joking with a friend about not sticking to it.
daily.example: I started a diet, and here I am eating ramen in the middle of the night.

daily.title: Reacting to the news
daily.description: Commenting on a news story.
daily.example: The response was slow, and in the end people even died.

work.title: Reviewing a failed project
work.description: Looking back in a meeting at how a project got worse step by step.
work.example: The specs kept changing, and in the end we couldn't even meet the deadline.

work.title: Reporting a corporate scandal
work.description: News commentary on a company's poor response.
work.example: The company kept changing its explanation, and in the end it even canceled the press conference.

etymology: 「始末」 comes from Chinese: 「始」 (beginning) and 「末」 (end) mean the whole course of events, and so the outcome. 「始末だ」 means “the outcome is ...”, and later came to be used only for bad outcomes.

similar.title: 〜あげく
similar.explanation: 〜あげく follows the cause and stresses “after a long time of ...”. 〜始末だ comes at the end of the sentence and points straight at the frustrating final state, with stronger blame.

similar.title: 〜末(に)
similar.explanation: 〜末に is a neutral “after ..., finally”; the result can be good or bad. 〜始末だ is only for bad results.

similar.title: 〜結果
similar.explanation: 〜結果 states a result objectively. 〜始末だ carries the speaker's frustration and resignation.

meaning: You want to do something but have no way or means to do it; there's nothing you can do.
connection: Verb dictionary form + すべがない／すべもない (written 「術」 in kanji)

senses.label: No way to
senses.meaning: There's no method or means to do what you want. Like “there's no way to ...” or “can't possibly ...”. More literary than 「方法がない」, with a sense of helplessness.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + すべがない／すべはない／すべがなかった (common: 知る・伝える・防ぐ・確かめる)
examples: There's no way to know where he is now.
I had no way to express how I felt.
There's no way to confirm whether that story is true.

senses.label: Helpless
senses.meaning: 「なす術もない」 and 「なす術もなく」 are set phrases: completely helpless in the face of a disaster, a strong opponent, and so on. 「も」 is stronger than 「が」.
senses.connection: なす + 術もない／術もなく
examples: People were helpless before the tsunami.
Up against a powerhouse team, we lost without putting up a fight.

notes: 「すべ」 is written 「術」 and read 「すべ」, not 「じゅつ」.
It's quite literary. In speech people usually say 「〜方法がない」 or 「〜しようがない」.
Don't confuse it with 「すべて」 (all).

daily.title: Lost touch with an old friend
daily.description: Talking to family about a friend from years ago.
daily.example: He moved away, and now I have no way to contact him.

daily.title: Watching disaster news
daily.description: Reacting to a flood report.
daily.example: Houses were swept away by the muddy water, and the residents were helpless.

work.title: Explaining a stalled investigation
work.description: Reporting to a boss that information can't be verified.
work.example: No records remain, so there's no way to confirm what the situation was at the time.

work.title: Sports news
work.description: Reporting a one-sided match.
work.example: Japan was pinned back the whole game and lost helplessly.

etymology: 「すべ」 (術) is a native Japanese word meaning “means, method”. Old Japanese already had phrases like 「せむすべなし」 (nothing to be done). Today it survives mainly in set expressions like 「〜すべがない」 and 「なす術もない」.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: 〜ようがない follows the verb ます-stem and is common in both speech and writing. 〜すべがない follows the dictionary form and is more formal and literary.

similar.title: 〜ほかない・〜よりほかない
similar.explanation: 〜よりほかない means “have no choice but to ...”. 〜すべがない means “there's no way to ...”: you can't do it.

similar.title: 〜ほかしかたがない
similar.explanation: 「〜ほかしかたがない」 means only one option is left. 〜すべがない means there's no option at all.

meaning: 「ただ」 and 「のみ」 work together to strongly limit the scope: “only ...”, “nothing but ...”.
connection: ただ + noun / verb dictionary form + のみ（だ）

senses.label: All one can do is
senses.meaning: There's nothing else to do but this. Like “all I can do is ...” or “the only thing left is to ...”. Often sounds determined or resigned.
senses.connection: ただ + verb dictionary form + のみだ／のみです (common: 待つ・祈る・進む・努力する)
examples: I've done everything I can. All that's left is to wait for the results.
All we can do is move forward.
Right now, all I can do is pray that everyone is safe.

senses.label: Only this
senses.meaning: Limits a noun or number: “just this, nothing more”. Like “only ...” or “just ...”. More formal than 「だけ」.
senses.connection: ただ + noun / number + のみ
examples: Only one person passed the exam.
The only thing on his mind is winning.

notes: Both 「ただ」 and 「のみ」 mean “only”. Used together, the limiting effect is very strong.
Used in writing and speeches. In conversation people say 「ただ〜だけ」.
「ただ〜のみならず」 means “not only ...”, almost the opposite. Don't mix them up.

daily.title: After an exam
daily.description: A student tells a friend how they feel.
daily.example: It's over now, so all I can do is pray I passed.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: The hero makes up his mind.
daily.example: I have no doubts. I will simply walk my own path.

work.title: Pre-game interview
work.description: An athlete speaks to reporters.
work.example: We're fully prepared. All that's left is to give it everything we've got.

work.title: Company speech
work.description: The president speaks at a year-end event.
work.example: All we can do is keep working with integrity.

etymology: 「ただ」 (唯・只) is an adverb meaning “only”. 「のみ」 is often said to come from old 「の＋身」, meaning “just”. Both are limiting words, and stacking them adds emphasis.

similar.title: 〜のみ
similar.explanation: 〜のみ alone is already a formal “only”. Adding 「ただ」 makes the limit stronger, and it's often used to express determination.

similar.title: 〜だけ
similar.explanation: 「ただ〜だけ」 is the conversational version. 「ただ〜のみ」 is more formal and dignified.

similar.title: 〜までだ
similar.explanation: 〜までだ means “if worst comes to worst, I'll just ...”, with a sense of going all in. ただ〜のみ simply stresses there's nothing else.

meaning: Not limited to the first item; it extends to the second as well. Like “not just ... (but also ...)”.
connection: ただ + noun / plain form + のみならず

senses.label: Not only this thing
senses.meaning: A problem, effect, etc. isn't limited to the first item but covers a wider range. Like “not just ..., but also ...”. More formal and solemn than 「〜だけでなく」. The second part often has 「も」, 「まで」, or 「全体」.
senses.connection: ただ + noun + のみならず、〜も (common: 日本・個人・国内・若者)
examples: Environmental problems are not just one country's issue, but a challenge for the whole world.
This law will have a big impact not only on companies but also on individuals.

senses.label: Not only did ...
senses.meaning: After a verb or adjective: it's not only this fact, there's something more. Often used to praise or to stress how serious something is. A slightly less stiff version is 「ただ〜のみでなく」.
senses.connection: ただ + verb / い-adjective plain form, or な-adjective + である + のみならず; ただ〜のみでなく
examples: He's not only a great singer, he's also a talented composer.
That remark not only hurt the other person, it also damaged the company's reputation.
Reading doesn't just give you knowledge; it also enriches your heart.

notes: 「ただ」 strengthens 「のみならず」 and makes “not only” stand out more. There's also an even more classical form, 「ただに〜のみならず」.
Put 「のみならず」 directly after a noun, without 「だ」. With な-adjectives use 「〜であるのみならず」.
It looks like 「ただ〜のみ」 (only), but the meaning is the opposite. Check whether 「ならず」 follows.

daily.title: News commentary
daily.description: A commentator talks about a social issue.
daily.example: The falling birthrate is serious not only in rural areas but in cities too.

daily.title: Reading a biography
daily.description: A biography describes someone's achievements.
daily.example: He made his name not only as a doctor but also as a writer.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper explains the value of its research.
work.example: This study is significant not only in theory but also in practice.

work.title: Corporate speech
work.description: A president stresses the company's social responsibility.
work.example: We must not only pursue profit but also contribute to society.

etymology: 「のみならず」 is made of the limiting particle 「のみ」 + 「ならず」, the negative of the classical copula 「なり」, literally “not being only ...”. The adverb 「ただ」 (唯) adds emphasis. It's a formal style that comes from reading classical Chinese texts in Japanese.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Same meaning. With 「ただ」 it's stronger and more solemn, often seen in speeches and papers.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: 〜ばかりでなく works in speech and writing. ただ〜のみならず is the most formal.

similar.title: 〜にとどまらず
similar.explanation: 〜にとどまらず stresses “it didn't stay within a range but spread beyond it”. ただ〜のみならず simply adds: “not only ... but also ...”.

similar.title: 〜はおろか
similar.explanation: With 〜はおろか, the first item is the obvious case, and the second is often an extreme negative example. ただ〜のみならず has no such contrast in degree.

meaning: Something is serious: it can't be settled with just a certain level of response or attitude, and heavier consequences or responsibility will follow.
connection: Noun / plain form + ではすまない／ではすまされない

senses.label: Won't be enough
senses.meaning: The first item (an apology, a joke, something minor) won't settle the matter. Like “... won't cut it” or “it's not something you can settle with just ...”. Suggests more serious consequences.
senses.connection: Noun + では済まない (common: 冗談・謝罪・ごめん・笑い事); verb dictionary form + だけでは済まない
examples: This is no longer a problem you can laugh off.
With damage this widespread, an apology alone probably won't be enough.
If you make another mistake, you won't get off with a warning.

senses.label: Can't be excused
senses.meaning: 「〜ではすまされない」 uses the passive to stress that society or others won't let it end with just ... . Often used when holding someone responsible. 「知らなかったではすまされない」 is a common phrase.
senses.connection: Plain form (quoted) / noun + では済まされない
examples: “I didn't know” is no excuse.
Misconduct by public officials can't be dismissed as a personal matter.

notes: 「済む」 means “to be settled, to be resolved”. The positive 「〜で済む」 means “... is enough to settle it”; this pattern is its negative.
「ないではすまない」 (have to ...) is a different pattern, 「〜ずにはすまない」. Don't mix them up.
In speech people often say 「〜じゃすまない」 or 「〜じゃすまされない」.

daily.title: Parent scolding a child
daily.description: The child broke a neighbor's window.
daily.example: You broke someone's window. “Sorry” isn't going to cut it.

daily.title: Reacting to the news
daily.description: Commenting on a traffic accident report.
daily.example: Drunk driving can't be excused as a careless mistake.

work.title: Boss warning a subordinate
work.description: The subordinate made a serious error in a contract.
work.example: A mistake in the contract amount won't be settled with a written apology.

work.title: Corporate crisis response
work.description: The company discusses a data leak.
work.example: A leak of personal information is not something an apology alone can settle.

etymology: 「すむ」 (済む) originally means “to end, to be settled”. 「〜で済む」 is “settled with ...”; in the negative it becomes 「〜では済まない」, and the passive 「済まされない」 stresses that others won't allow it.

similar.title: 〜ずにはすまない
similar.explanation: 〜ずにはすまない follows the negative form of a verb: “you have to ... (it's only right)”. 〜ではすまない follows nouns etc.: “... won't settle it”.

similar.title: 〜で済む
similar.explanation: 「〜で済む」 is the positive form: “... is enough, gets it over with”, as in 「軽いけがで済んだ」.

similar.title: 〜てはならない
similar.explanation: 〜てはならない expresses prohibition. 〜ではすまされない means once it's done, responsibility can't be easily brushed off.

meaning: To reach a goal, someone goes so far as to use extreme measures they normally wouldn't.
connection: Verb te-form + まで; noun + までして

senses.label: Go so far as to
senses.meaning: To achieve something, someone even does what people normally wouldn't. Like “go so far as to ...”. The second part is usually the speaker's judgment, such as 「〜たくない」, 「〜必要はない」, 「〜とは」, showing surprise or disapproval.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + まで (common: 借金して・徹夜して・嘘をついて・並んで)
examples: I wouldn't go into debt just to buy designer goods.
He even lied to his parents to go to that concert.
Is it really worth lining up for hours just to eat it?

senses.label: Even go as far as
senses.meaning: Noun + までして: someone even did something extreme. 「そこまでして」 means “going that far”. Often sounds surprised or puzzled.
senses.connection: Noun + までして; そこまでして／あそこまでして
examples: I even stayed up all night preparing, but the meeting was canceled.
Do you want to win that badly? (going that far?)

notes: The first part is a cost paid or an extreme measure, not an ordinary action.
The second part is usually a negative judgment: 「〜てまで〜したくない」, 「〜てまで〜する必要はない」.
It's the same pattern as N2's 「〜まで（して）」. At N1 it's often tested against 「〜てでも」.

daily.title: Talking about lines
daily.description: A friend invites you to a place with a long line.
daily.example: I don't want to wait two hours just to eat.

daily.title: Talking about dieting
daily.description: A friend is dieting so hard it's hurting her health.
daily.example: There's no need to wreck your health just to lose weight.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Someone does anything to go viral.
daily.example: I can't understand people risking danger just to shoot a video.

work.title: Talking about work style
work.description: A senior colleague warns a junior about overtime.
work.example: You shouldn't work at the cost of your health.

work.title: News on a scandal
work.description: Reporting a company's data fraud.
work.example: The company even falsified data to try to win the contract.

etymology: 「まで」 is a particle marking an end point or limit. “Reaching the limit of ...” came to mean “even to the extent of ...”. With the te-form or 「して」, it means pushing your methods to the extreme to reach a goal.

similar.title: 〜まで(して)・〜てまで
similar.explanation: The same pattern as listed at N2, with the same meaning.

similar.title: 〜てでも
similar.explanation: 〜てでも shows the speaker's strong will: “I'll do it even if I have to ...”. 〜てまで is mostly used to judge (often negatively) excessive measures by others or oneself.

similar.title: 〜まで (even)
similar.explanation: 「まで」 alone means “even ...”, adding an extreme example. 〜てまで stresses paying a price to reach a goal.

meaning: Because of one's face, position, or what one has already said or done, one has to (or can't) act a certain way.
connection: Noun + の / verb plain form + 手前

senses.label: Having said that
senses.meaning: After something you've already said or done: to save face, you can't back out now. Like “since I already ...” or “having said so ...”. Often followed by 「〜わけにはいかない」 or 「〜しかない」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + 手前 (common: 言った・約束した・引き受けた・大口をたたいた)
examples: Since I promised I'd definitely go, I can't back out now.
I volunteered for it myself, so I can't quit halfway.

senses.label: In front of
senses.meaning: After a person or a situation: in front of others, you must watch what you say or do. Like “in front of ...” or “out of regard for ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + の手前; verb ている-form + 手前
examples: We try not to argue in front of the kids.
With my team watching, I couldn't show any weakness.

notes: 「手前」 is also an ordinary noun meaning “just before, this side”, as in 「駅の手前で降りる」. That's not this pattern.
The second part is usually “can't ...” or “have no choice but to ...”, showing the speaker feels bound by their position.
「手前味噌」 (blowing one's own horn) is a separate idiom.

daily.title: Going reluctantly
daily.description: You told a friend you'd go but now don't want to.
daily.example: Well, I said I'd go, so I guess I have to.

daily.title: In front of the kids
daily.description: A parent explains why they don't smoke at home.
daily.example: For the kids' sake, I decided to quit smoking.

work.title: Project leader
work.description: Hitting trouble after volunteering.
work.example: I raised my hand for this, so I can't complain.

work.title: Being mindful of clients
work.description: Handling a problem with a client present.
work.example: With the client there, I didn't say anything at the time.

etymology: 「手前」 originally means “at hand, right in front”, the area near you. It came to mean “in front of someone's eyes”, and then “one's face or standing in front of others”.

similar.title: 〜以上(は)
similar.explanation: 〜以上は means “since ..., (I must)”, stressing logical responsibility. 〜手前 stresses face and how others see you.

similar.title: 〜からには
similar.explanation: 〜からには usually shows determination (since ..., I'll see it through). 〜手前 usually shows feeling forced or awkward.

similar.title: 〜上は
similar.explanation: 〜上は is formal: having decided, you must take it on. 〜手前 focuses more on face in relationships.

title: 〜というもの (period of time)
meaning: After a word for a period of time, stresses that a state continued throughout that long period.
connection: Noun for a period + というもの

senses.label: For the whole ...
senses.meaning: Stresses “for this long”, a state continued the whole time. Like “for the past ...” or “all this ...”. The speaker feels the time was long and sounds moved or weary. Often preceded by 「この」 or 「ここ」.
senses.connection: (この／ここ) + period noun + というもの (common: 一週間・一か月・数年・十年)
examples: I've barely slept this whole past week.
For the past few years, I haven't heard a thing from him.
The three months since I was hospitalized felt really long.

notes: The second part is a continuing state, not a one-time action.
「それが人生というものだ」 is a different pattern, 「〜というものだ」 (that's how it is). Don't mix them up.
「〜てからというもの」 means “ever since ... (it's been)”, a related set phrase.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: You've been busy for a while.
daily.example: This whole past month, I haven't had a single day off.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character's longing is described.
daily.example: In all these ten years, not a day has gone by that I haven't thought of her.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting days of unusual weather.
work.example: For the past week, record-breaking heat has continued across the country.

work.title: Explaining background in a meeting
work.description: Explaining a long sales slump.
work.example: For the past six months, sales have remained sluggish.

etymology: 「というもの」 is quoting 「と言う」 + the formal noun 「もの」, originally “the thing called ...”. After a period word, it treats that stretch of time as one whole and stresses how long it was.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: 〜てからというもの takes an event as the starting point: things changed from then on. Period + というもの just stresses the length of time.

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: 〜にわたって objectively describes a span of time or area. 〜というもの carries the feeling “for so long, ...”.

similar.title: 〜というものだ
similar.explanation: 〜というものだ means “that's just how ... is”, a judgment. Period + というもの stresses a time period.

meaning: Gives two typical examples to say it applies everywhere, without distinction. Like “whether it's ... or ..., everywhere (always) ...”.
connection: Noun A + といわず、noun B + といわず

senses.label: Both A and B, everywhere
senses.meaning: Gives two examples of the same kind to say it's not just them; the whole thing is in that state. Like “both ... and ..., all over”. Often describes something surprising or unpleasant.
senses.connection: Noun A + といわず + noun B + といわず (common: 顔・手, 昼・夜, 家の中・外)
examples: The kids were covered in mud, face, hands, everything.
Day and night, the construction noise is loud.
Inside the trains and in the stations, everywhere was packed with people.

senses.label: Don't wait until
senses.meaning: 「〜といわず」 alone, after a time word: “don't wait until ...; (do it) now”. Often paired with 「今すぐ」 or 「今日にでも」 to urge quick action.
senses.connection: Time noun + といわず (common: 明日・来週・来年)
examples: Don't wait until tomorrow. You should go to the hospital today.
Why wait until next year? Let's start this year.

notes: A and B are concrete things of the same kind, standing for “all”.
It's fairly literary. In conversation people say 「〜も〜も」.
Ordinary negatives of 「言う」, like 「何も言わず」 (without saying anything), are not this pattern.

daily.title: Describing a naughty cat
daily.description: Telling a friend about your cat.
daily.example: Our cat shreds everything with its claws, the sofa, the curtains, you name it.

daily.title: Urging a friend to see a doctor
daily.description: Your friend feels ill but keeps putting it off.
daily.example: Don't wait for the weekend. Go get checked today.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes the hero's busy life.
daily.example: Holidays or weekdays, he was absorbed in his research.

work.title: Disaster news
work.description: Reporting the scene after a typhoon.
work.example: Roads and fields alike are all under water.

work.title: Reporting frequent failures
work.description: Telling the boss about system problems.
work.example: Errors are occurring morning and night.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + 「言わず」, the classical negative of 「言う」. Literally “without calling it A, without calling it B”, i.e. “whether you call it A or B”, which came to mean “A and B alike, everything”.

similar.title: 〜といい〜といい
similar.explanation: 〜といい〜といい gives two aspects to evaluate something (praise or criticism). 〜といわず〜といわず stresses that the whole range is in some state, without evaluating.

similar.title: 〜に限らず
similar.explanation: 〜に限らず means “not limited to ...” and gives one example. 〜といわず〜といわず gives two examples to mean “everywhere”.

similar.title: 〜を問わず
similar.explanation: 〜を問わず usually follows opposite pairs like “men and women, age, day and night”: “regardless of”. 〜といわず〜といわず follows concrete things and describes a concrete state.

meaning: Written style: “even ...”, “even if ...”. Usually followed by a negative or discouraging result.
connection: Noun + とて; verb た-form + とて; 〜からとて

senses.label: Even someone
senses.meaning: Names a person or thing and says even it is no exception. Like “even ...” or “... is no different”. Stiffer and more formal than 「〜でも」. Common in 「私とて」 and 「誰とて」.
senses.connection: Noun + とて (common: 私・彼・親・大人・プロ・誰)
examples: Even I feel just as frustrated as everyone else.
Even veteran doctors make mistakes sometimes.
There's no one, whoever they are, who doesn't fear death.

senses.label: Even if you did
senses.meaning: Even if you do the first thing, you won't get the result you want. Like “even if ..., (it's no use)”. The second part is usually negative or futile, often with 「いくら」 or 「今さら」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + とて
examples: Even if you apologize now, you probably won't be forgiven.
No matter how much we hurry, we won't make it now.
Crying won't change anything.

senses.label: Just because
senses.meaning: 「〜からとて」 equals 「〜からといって」: “just because ... doesn't mean ...”. The second part is usually negative or a prohibition. It's an old-fashioned, literary form.
senses.connection: Plain form + からとて
examples: You shouldn't spoil children just because they're children.
Being busy doesn't mean it's OK to break promises.

notes: It's formal and literary. In speech, use 「〜だって」, 「〜たって」, or 「〜からといって」 instead.
The 「とて」 in 「とても」 (very) has nothing to do with this pattern.
「〜こととて」 shows a reason (because ...) and is a different pattern.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Your friend failed an exam; you've failed before too.
daily.example: I've failed plenty of times myself, you know.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character's inner monologue.
daily.example: Even if I regret it now, she won't come back.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting that even big companies face crises.
work.example: Even big companies can't survive if they can't adapt to change.

work.title: Formal speech
work.description: A manager stresses the rules at a meeting.
work.example: Being an executive doesn't make you an exception to the rules.

etymology: 「とて」 is the quoting particle 「と」 + the conjunctive particle 「て」, originally meaning 「と言って」 or 「と思って」. It later took on a concessive meaning, “even if you say ...”. In classical Japanese, 「〜とて」 could also show purpose or reason.

similar.title: 〜といえども
similar.explanation: 〜といえども is more formal, common in law and speeches. 〜とて is a bit more emotional and often found in literature.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: 〜ても is the ordinary “even if”, used in speech and writing. Verb た-form + とて is literary, and the second part is usually futile.

similar.title: 〜こととて
similar.explanation: 〜こととて shows a reason (since it's ...), unlike the concessive meaning of this pattern.

similar.title: 〜からといって
similar.explanation: 〜からとて is the literary, old-fashioned form of 〜からといって, with the same meaning.

meaning: Shows a sudden, complete change compared with how things were before.
connection: Noun + とはうってかわって (打って変わって)

senses.label: Completely different from
senses.meaning: Things have totally changed compared with before. Like “in sharp contrast to ...” or “unlike ...”. Often used for sudden changes in weather, attitude, mood, or situation. Often preceded by 「昨日」, 「以前」, 「前回」.
senses.connection: Noun + とは打って変わって (common: 昨日・以前・前半・普段)
examples: Unlike yesterday, it's been a beautiful day since this morning.
He's a changed man and is working hard now.
In the second half, in sharp contrast to the first, Japan went on the attack.

senses.label: Transformed
senses.meaning: 「打って変わった + noun」 modifies a noun: “a totally changed ...”. 「打って変わり」 is used to link clauses. Both stress how fast and how big the change is.
senses.connection: 打って変わった + noun; 打って変わり、〜
examples: After being scolded, he sat there, suddenly very quiet.
At night the town was transformed, wrapped in silence.

notes: Used for sudden, complete changes, not slow gradual ones.
The kanji is 「打って変わって」, but it's often written in kana. 「打って」 just adds emphasis; it doesn't mean “hit”.
The change can be good or bad, but it's usually to the exact opposite state.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: The day after a heavy storm, it cleared up.
daily.example: What a change from yesterday's downpour. It's totally clear.

daily.title: A friend has changed
daily.description: A friend changed after starting a relationship.
daily.example: Since he got a girlfriend, he's become so much more cheerful than before.

work.title: Stock market news
work.description: The market suddenly turned around.
work.example: In contrast to the previous day, stock prices rose sharply.

work.title: Evaluating in a meeting
work.description: Assessing the change a new manager brought.
work.example: Since the new structure began, the workplace has a completely different atmosphere.

etymology: 「打って変わる」 is 「打つ」 + 「変わる」. Here 「打つ」 is an intensifying prefix meaning “suddenly, completely”, so the whole means “to change completely all at once”.

similar.title: 〜にひきかえ
similar.explanation: 〜にひきかえ contrasts two different things (A vs. B). 〜とはうってかわって compares the same thing before and after.

similar.title: 〜に反して
similar.explanation: 〜に反して means contrary to expectations or wishes. 〜とはうってかわって means opposite to the previous state.

similar.title: 〜とは違って
similar.explanation: 「〜とは違って」 just says “different”. 〜とはうってかわって stresses a dramatic change, like a different person.

meaning: Expresses a minimal hope, “even just a little”; after a question word, it means “any ... at all”.
connection: Noun/adverb of small amount + なりとも; question word + なりと（も）

senses.label: Even a little
senses.meaning: Names a bare minimum: “even just this much would be good”. Like “even a little” or “at least somewhat”. The second part is usually a wish, intention, or request.
senses.connection: 少し・多少・わずか・一目・一日 etc. + なりとも
examples: I'd be glad if I can be of even a little help to you all.
I want to see my mother, even if only for a moment.
I want to help the disaster area, even if only a little.

senses.label: Anything at all
senses.meaning: After a question word: “any ... is fine”. Like “anything at all” or “anywhere”. 「何なりと」 is common in customer service.
senses.connection: 何・誰・どこへ + なりと（も）
examples: If you need anything, please don't hesitate to ask.
Go wherever you like.

notes: 「なりとも」 is formal and polite. In conversation people say 「〜でも」 or 「せめて〜でも」.
「何なりとお申し付けください」 is a polite phrase common in the service industry.
Don't confuse it with 「〜なり〜なり」 (either ... or ...) or 「〜なり」 (as soon as).

daily.title: Visiting someone in hospital
daily.description: You want to visit a friend in hospital.
daily.example: Even if it's just for a short time, I want to go see him.

daily.title: Hotel front desk
daily.description: A staff member speaks to a guest.
daily.example: If there's anything at all, please let us know.

work.title: Ending a business email
work.description: A modest line when attaching documents.
work.example: I hope this material will be of some help to you.

work.title: Charity event speech
work.description: Asking people to donate.
work.example: We would be grateful for any support, however small.

etymology: 「なり」 is a remnant of the classical copula 「なり」, and 「とも」 is a conjunctive particle for concessive conditions. Together they literally mean “even if it's ...”, which came to mean “even if only ...”.

similar.title: せめて〜でも
similar.explanation: 「せめて〜でも」 is common in speech too. 〜なりとも is more formal and polite, used in speeches and letters.

similar.title: 〜たりとも
similar.explanation: 〜たりとも follows 「一 + counter」 and takes a negative: “not even one ...”. 〜なりとも takes a wish: “even a little would be good”.

similar.title: 〜なり〜なり
similar.explanation: 〜なり〜なり offers choices: “either ... or ...”. 〜なりとも is a minimal wish.

meaning: Something isn't worth it or there's no need to react that way. Like “there's no need to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + には当たらない

senses.label: No need to
senses.meaning: The situation isn't serious enough to call for that reaction. Like “there's no need to ...” or “it's not worth ...”. Often used to tell someone not to be surprised, worried, critical, etc. Usually with verbs of judgment or feeling.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + には当たらない (common: 驚く・悲観する・非難する・心配する・感心する)
examples: His win reflects his true ability; it's nothing to be surprised about.
There's no need to be pessimistic over one failure.
His decision was unavoidable; there's no reason to criticize him.

notes: The first part is usually a verb of feeling or judgment, like 「驚く」, 「嘆く」, 「責める」, 「称賛する」.
Noun + 「に当たる」 can also mean “to amount to, to constitute”, as in 「違法行為には当たらない」 (does not constitute an illegal act). That's a different meaning.
「日光には当たらない」 (not exposed to sunlight) uses the literal meaning of 「当たる」, not this pattern.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is worried their child did badly on a test.
daily.example: He's only in first grade. There's no need to worry.

daily.title: News commentary
daily.description: A commentator talks about rising prices.
daily.example: A price rise this small is nothing to make a fuss about.

work.title: Speaking at a meeting
work.description: A department head reassures staff anxious about falling sales.
work.example: This is just a temporary dip; there's no need to be pessimistic.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: An editorial assesses a policy's effect.
work.example: This result was within expectations and is hardly surprising.

etymology: 「当たる」 originally means “to hit, to strike”, and came to mean “to correspond to, to be appropriate”. 「〜には当たらない」 means “doesn't call for ...”, and so “not worth, no need”.

similar.title: 〜までもない
similar.explanation: 〜までもない means “it's simple, no need to bother”. 〜には当たらない means “it's not serious (or it's reasonable), so it doesn't deserve that reaction”.

similar.title: 〜ことはない
similar.explanation: 〜ことはない is common in speech and directly tells someone they needn't do something. 〜には当たらない is more formal and sounds like an assessment.

similar.title: 〜には及ばない
similar.explanation: 〜には及ばない usually means “no need to go to the trouble” (e.g. 「お越しいただくには及びません」). 〜には当たらない usually follows verbs of emotional reaction.

meaning: Doing something ahead of others, other places, or another event; taking the lead.
connection: Noun + に先駆けて／に先駆け／に先駆けた + noun

senses.label: Ahead of
senses.meaning: Getting ahead of others of the same kind and doing something first. Like “ahead of ...” or “leading ...”. Usually a positive, pioneering act. Often after 「他社」, 「全国」, 「世界」, 「業界」.
senses.connection: Noun + に先駆けて (common: 他社・全国・世界・業界・他国)
examples: The company launched a new service ahead of its competitors.
This city was the first in the country to introduce fees for garbage collection.
Ahead of the public opening, a preview was held for the press.

senses.label: Leading, pioneering
senses.meaning: 「〜に先駆けた + noun」 modifies a noun: “pioneering ..., ahead of ...”. 「〜に先駆け、」 is a formal way to link clauses.
senses.connection: Noun + に先駆けた + noun; noun + に先駆け、〜
examples: This is a groundbreaking initiative, the first in the industry.
Japan put this technology into practical use ahead of the rest of the world.

notes: Mostly used in news, business, and other formal contexts.
It stresses being a pioneer, ahead of others, not just coming earlier in time. For simple order, use 「〜に先立って」.
「先駆け」 can also be a noun on its own, meaning “forerunner”, as in 「春の先駆け」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news introduces a new product launch.
daily.example: The new smartphone will go on sale in Japan before overseas.

daily.title: Talking about your hometown
daily.description: Describing a local policy.
daily.example: My town was the first in the country to make school lunches free.

work.title: Press release
work.description: A company announces a new product.
work.example: Ahead of the rest of the industry, we have developed an AI-powered diagnostic system.

work.title: Industry report
work.description: Analyzing policy trends in different countries.
work.example: The Nordic countries have pushed decarbonization policies ahead of other nations.

etymology: 「先駆け」 (さきがけ) originally meant being the first to charge into the enemy lines, from 「先に駆ける」. It came to mean “taking the lead, pioneer”, so 「〜に先駆けて」 means “charging out in front of ...”.

similar.title: 〜に先立って
similar.explanation: 〜に先立って means “before ... (preparing first)”, focusing on time order. 〜に先駆けて stresses being ahead of others, with a pioneering sense.

similar.title: 〜を皮切りに
similar.explanation: 〜を皮切りに means a series of events starts with something. 〜に先駆けて only stresses getting there first.

similar.title: 〜より先に
similar.explanation: 「〜より先に」 is the conversational “before ...”. 〜に先駆けて is formal and has a positive sense of leading.

meaning: Judging something against a standard, such as laws, rules, or experience.
connection: Noun + に照らして／に照らし／に照らせば

senses.label: In light of a standard
senses.meaning: Uses laws, rules, common sense, etc. as a yardstick and makes a judgment. Like “in light of ...” or “according to ...”. Mostly for formal judgments and decisions.
senses.connection: Noun + に照らして／に照らし (common: 法律・規則・社会通念・基準・常識)
examples: Judged in light of the law, what he did is illegal.
The disciplinary action was decided in accordance with company rules.
By common social standards, that demand is unreasonable.

senses.label: Checking against experience or facts
senses.meaning: Uses past experience, facts, or records as a reference to infer or check. 「〜に照らせば」 and 「〜に照らすと」 mean “judging by ...”. 「照らし合わせる」 means “to cross-check”.
senses.connection: Noun + に照らせば／に照らすと; 〜を〜に照らし合わせる
examples: Judging by past experience, this plan should succeed.
Check the invoice against the purchase order.

notes: Written style, common in legal, administrative, and business documents.
What comes before is the standard for judging, not just source material. For “based on data”, use 「〜に基づいて」.
「ライトで照らす」 (to light up with a light) is the literal meaning of 「照らす」, not this pattern.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news reports a court ruling.
daily.example: The court, in light of the law, found the defendant not guilty.

daily.title: Advising a friend
daily.description: Giving advice from your own experience.
daily.example: From my own experience, I think it's better not to make a move right now.

work.title: Compliance review
work.description: The legal department reviews a contract.
work.example: We have confirmed that this contract has no issues under the relevant laws and regulations.

work.title: Annual review
work.description: HR explains how evaluations work.
work.example: Evaluations will be carried out fairly, according to company standards.

etymology: 「照らす」 originally means “to shine light on”. It came to mean holding something up to the light to compare it, so 「〜に照らして」 means “looking at it in the light of ...”, measuring by a standard.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: 〜に基づいて means doing something based on data or facts. 〜に照らして means measuring against a standard to judge whether it's appropriate.

similar.title: 〜に即して
similar.explanation: 〜に即して means acting in line with the actual situation or rules. 〜に照らして focuses on judging after comparing.

similar.title: 〜にのっとって
similar.explanation: 〜にのっとって means following rules or tradition when doing something. 〜に照らして means using rules as a yardstick to judge.
